four that don’t say, ‘Enough!’:272829 ✦16 Sheol, the barren womb, the earth30 that is not satisfied with water31, and the fire that doesn’t say, ‘Enough!’32 ✦17 “The eye that mocks at his father, and scorns obedience to his mother, the ravens of the valley shall pick it out, the young eagles shall eat it.33 ✦18 “There are three things which are too amazing for me, four which I don’t understand:34 ✦19 The way of an eagle in the air, the way of a serpent35 on a rock, the way of a ship in the middle of the sea, and the way of a man36 with a maiden.37 ✦20 “So is the way of an adulterous woman38: She eats and wipes her mouth, and says, ‘I have done nothing wrong.’39 21 “For three things the earth40 trembles, and under four, it can’t bear up:41 ✦22 For a servant when he is king, a fool when he is filled with food,42 ✦23 for an unloved woman43 when she is married, and a servant who is heir to her mistress.44 24 “There are four things which are little on the earth45, but they are exceedingly wise:46 ✦25 The ants are not a strong people, yet they provide their food in the summer.47 ✦26 The hyraxes are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks.4849 ✦27 The locusts have no king, yet they advance in ranks.50 ✦28 You can catch a lizard with your hands, yet it is in kings’ palaces.51 ✦29 “There are three things which are stately in their march, four which are stately in going:52 ✦30 The lion, which is mightiest among animals, and doesn’t turn away for any;53 ✦31 the greyhound; the male goat; and the king against whom there is no rising up.5455 32 “If you have done foolishly in lifting up yourself, or if you have thought evil, put your hand over your mouth. 33 For as the churning of milk produces butter, and the wringing of the nose produces blood56, so the forcing of wrath produces strife.”

BOOK XXXIV

The Wisdom of Solomon

❖

The Wisdom of Solomon is recognized as Deuterocanonical Scripture by the Roman Catholic, Greek Orthodox, and Russian Orthodox Churches.

4647✦

1

1 Love1 righteousness2, all you who are judges of the earth3. Think of the Lord4 with a good5 mind. Seek him in singleness of heart6, 2 because he is found by those who don’t put him to the test, and is manifested to those who trust him. 3 for crooked thoughts separate from God7. His Power convicts when it is tested, and exposes the foolish; 4 because wisdom8 will not enter into a soul9 that devises evil, nor dwell in a body that is enslaved by sin10. 5 For a holy11 spirit12 of discipline will flee deceit, and will depart from thoughts that are without understanding, and will be ashamed when unrighteousness has come in. 6 For wisdom13 is a spirit14 who loves man, and she will not hold a blasphemer guiltless for his lips, because God15 is witness of his inmost self, and is a true overseer of his heart16, and a hearer of his tongue. 7 Because the spirit of the Lord17 has filled the world, and that which holds all things together knows what is said.18 8 Therefore no one who utters unrighteous things will be unseen; neither will Justice, when it convicts, pass him by. 9 For in his counsels the ungodly will be searched out, and the sound of his words will come to the Lord19 to bring his lawless deeds to conviction; 10 because a jealous ear listens to all things, and the noise of murmurings is not hidden. 11 Beware then of unprofitable murmuring, and keep your tongue from slander; because no secret utterance will go on its way void, and a lying mouth destroys a soul20. 12 Don’t court death in the error of your life. Don’t draw destruction upon yourselves by the works of your hands; 13 because God21 didn’t make death, neither does he delight when the living perish. 14 For he created22 all things that they might have being. The generative powers of the world are wholesome, and there is no poison of destruction in them, nor has Hades royal dominion upon earth23; 15 for righteousness24 is immortal, 16 but ungodly men by their hands and their words summon death; deeming him a friend they pined away. They made a covenant25 with him, because they are worthy to belong with him.

2

1 For they said within themselves, with unsound reasoning, “Our life is short and sorrowful. There is no healing when a man1 comes to his end, and no one was ever known who was released from Hades. 2 Because we were born by mere chance, and hereafter we will be as though we had never been, because the breath2 in our nostrils is smoke, and reason is a spark kindled by the beating of our heart3, 3 which being extinguished, the body will be turned into ashes, and the spirit4 will be dispersed as thin air. 4 Our name will be forgotten in time. No one will remember our works. Our life will pass away as the traces of a cloud, and will be scattered as is a mist, when it is chased by the rays of the sun, and overcome by its heat.5 5 For our allotted time is the passing of a shadow, and our end doesn’t retreat, because it is securely sealed, and no one turns it back.6 6 “Come therefore and let’s enjoy the good7 things that exist. Let’s use the creation earnestly as in our youth. 7 Let’s fill ourselves with costly wine and perfumes, and let no spring flower pass us by. 8 Let’s crown ourselves with rosebuds before they wither. 9 Let none of us go without his share in our proud revelry. Let’s leave tokens of mirth everywhere, because this is our portion, and this is our lot. 10 Let’s oppress the righteous8 poor. Let’s not spare the widow, nor regard the gray hair of the old man9. 11 But let our strength be a law of righteousness; for that which is weak is proven useless. 12 But let’s lie in wait for the righteous10 man, because he annoys us, is contrary to our works, reproaches us with sins against the law, and charges us with sins against our training. 13 He professes to have knowledge of God11, and calls himself a child of the Lord12. 14 He became to us a reproof of our thoughts. 15 He is grievous to us even to look at, because his life is unlike other men’s, and his paths are strange. 16 We were regarded by him as something worthless, and he abstains from our ways as from uncleanness. He calls the latter end of the righteous happy. He boasts that God13 is his father. 17 Let’s see if his words are true. Let’s test what will happen at the end of his life. 18 For if the righteous man14 is God15’s son, he will uphold him, and he will deliver him out of the hand of his adversaries. 19 Let’s test him with insult and torture, that we may find out how gentle he is, and test his patience. 20 Let’s condemn him to a shameful death, for he will be protected, according to his words.” 21 Thus they reasoned, and they were led astray; for their wickedness blinded them, 22 and they didn’t know the mysteries of God16, neither did they hope for wages of holiness, nor did they discern that there is a prize for blameless souls.17 23 Because God18 created19 man20 for incorruption, and made him an image21 of his own everlastingness; 24 but death entered into the world by the envy of the devil, and those who belong to him experience it.

3

1 But the souls of the righteous1 are in the hand of God2, and no torment will touch them. 2 In the eyes of the foolish they seemed to have died. Their departure was considered a disaster, 3 and their travel away from us ruin, but they are in peace3. 4 For even if in the sight of men they are punished, their hope is full of immortality. 5 Having borne a little chastening, they will receive great good; because God4 tested them, and found them worthy of himself. 6 He tested them like gold in the furnace, and he accepted them as a whole burnt offering. 7 In the time of their visitation they will shine. They will run back and forth like sparks among stubble. 8 They will judge nations and have dominion over peoples. The Lord5 will reign over them forever. 9 Those who trust him will understand truth. The faithful will live with him in love6, because grace and mercy7 are with his chosen ones. 10 But the ungodly will be punished even as their reasoning deserves, those who neglected righteous8ness and revolted from the Lord9; 11 for he who despises wisdom10 and discipline is miserable. Their hope is void and their toils unprofitable. Their works are useless. 12 Their wives are foolish and their children are wicked. 13 Their descendants are cursed. For the barren woman who is undefiled is happy, she who has not conceived in transgression. She will have fruit when God examines souls. 14 So is the eunuch which has done no lawless deed with his hands, nor imagined wicked things against the Lord11; for a precious gift will be given to him for his faithfulness, and a delightful inheritance in the Lord’s sanctuary.12 15 For good13 labors have fruit of great renown. The root of understanding can’t fail.14 16 But children of adulterers will not come to maturity. The seed of an unlawful union will vanish away. 17 For if they live long, they will not be esteemed, and in the end, their old age will be without honor. 18 If they die young, they will have no hope, nor consolation in the day of judgment. 19 For the end of an unrighteous generation is always grievous.

4

1 It is better to be childless with virtue, for immortality is in the memory of virtue, because it is recognized both before God1 and before men. 2 When it is present, people imitate it. They long after it when it has departed. Throughout all time it marches, crowned in triumph, victorious in the competition for the prizes that are undefiled. 3 But the multiplying brood of the ungodly will be of no profit, and their illegitimate offshoots won’t take deep2 root, nor will they establish a sure hold. 4 For even if they grow branches and flourish for a season, standing unsure, they will be shaken by the wind3. They will be uprooted by the violence of winds. 5 Their branches will be broken off before they come to maturity. Their fruit will be useless, never ripe to eat, and fit for nothing. 6 For unlawfully conceived children are witnesses of wickedness against parents when they are investigated. 7 But a righteous4 man, even if he dies before his time, will be at rest. 8 For honorable old age is not that which stands in length of time, nor is its measure given by number of years, 9 but understanding is gray hair to men, and an unspotted life is ripe old age.5 10 Being found well-pleasing to God6, someone was loved. While living among sinners he was transported. 11 He was caught away, lest evil should change his understanding, or guile deceive his soul7. 12 For the fascination of wickedness obscures the things which are good, and the whirl of desire perverts an innocent mind. 13 Being made perfect quickly, he filled a long time; 14 for his soul8 was pleasing to the Lord9. Therefore he hurried out of the midst of wickedness. 15 But the peoples saw and didn’t understand, not considering this, that grace and mercy10 are with his chosen, and that he visits his holy ones; 16 but a righteous11 man who is dead will condemn the ungodly who are living, and youth who is quickly perfected will condemn the many years of an unrighteous man’s old age. 17 For the ungodly will see a wise man’s end, and won’t understand what the Lord12 planned for him, and why he safely kept him.13 18 They will see, and they will despise; but the Lord will laugh them to scorn. After this, they will become a dishonored carcass and a reproach among the dead forever;14 19 because he will dash them speechless to the ground, and will shake them from the foundations. They will lie utterly waste15. They will be in anguish and their memory will perish. 20 They will come with coward fear16 when their sins are counted. Their lawless deeds will convict them to their face.

5

1 Then the righteous1 man2 will stand in great boldness before the face of those who afflicted him, and those who make his labors of no account. 2 When they see him, they will be troubled with terrible fear3, and will be amazed at the marvel of salvation4. 3 They will speak among themselves repenting, and for distress of spirit5 they will groan, “This was he whom we used to hold in derision, as a parable of reproach. 4 We fools considered his life madness, and his end without honor. 5 How was he counted among sons of God6? How is his lot among saints? 6 Truly we went astray from the way of truth. The light7 of righteousness8 didn’t shine for us. The sun didn’t rise for us. 7 We took our fill of the paths of lawlessness and destruction. We traveled through trackless deserts, but we didn’t know the Lord9’s way. 8 What did our arrogance profit us? What good10 have riches and boasting brought us? 9 Those things all passed away as a shadow, like a rumor that runs by, 10 like a ship passing through the billowy water11, which, when it has gone by, there is no trace to be found, no pathway of its keel in the waves. 11 Or it is like when a bird flies through the air, no evidence of its passage is found, but the light12 wind, lashed with the stroke of its pinions, and torn apart with the violent rush of the moving wings, is passed through. Afterwards no sign of its coming remains. 12 Or it is like when an arrow is shot at a mark, the air it divided closes up again immediately, so that men don’t know where it passed through.13 13 So we also, as soon as we were born, ceased to be; and we had no sign of virtue to show, but we were utterly consumed in our wickedness.” 14 Because the hope of the ungodly man is like chaff carried by the wind14, and as foam vanishing before a tempest; and is scattered like smoke by the wind, and passes by as the remembrance of a guest who stays just a day.15 15 But the righteous16 live forever. Their reward is in the Lord17, and the care for them with the Most High. 16 Therefore they will receive the crown of royal dignity and the diadem of beauty from the Lord18’s hand, because he will cover them with his right hand, and he will shield them with his arm. 17 He will take his zeal as complete armor, and will make the whole creation his weapons to punish his enemies: 18 He will put on righteousness19 as a breastplate, and will wear impartial judgment as a helmet. 19 He will take holiness as an invincible shield. 20 He will sharpen stern wrath for a sword. The universe will go with him to fight against his frenzied foes. 21 Shafts of lightning will fly with true aim. They will leap to the mark from the clouds, as from a well-drawn bow. 22 Hailstones full of wrath will be hurled as from a catapult. The water20 of the sea will be angered against them. Rivers will sternly overwhelm them. 23 A mighty wind21 will encounter them. It will winnow them away like a tempest. So lawlessness will make all the land desolate. Their evil-doing will overturn the thrones of princes.

2223

6

1 Hear therefore, you kings, and understand. Learn, you judges of the ends of the earth1. 2 Give ear, you rulers who have dominion over many people, and make your boast in multitudes of nations,2 3 because your dominion was given to you from the Lord3, and your sovereignty from the Most High. He will search out your works, and will inquire about your plans, 4 because being officers of his kingdom, you didn’t judge rightly, nor did you keep the law, nor did you walk according to God4’s counsel. 5 He will come upon you awfully and swiftly, because a stern judgment comes on those who are in high places. 6 For the man of low estate may be pardoned in mercy5, but mighty men will be mightily tested. 7 For the Sovereign Lord6 of all will not be impressed with anyone, neither will he show deference to greatness; because it is he who made both small and great, and cares about them all;78 8 but the scrutiny that comes upon the powerful is strict. 9 Therefore, my words are to you, O princes, that you may learn wisdom9 and not fall away. 10 For those who have kept the things that are holy10 in holiness will be made holy. Those who have been taught them will find what to say in defense. 11 Therefore set your desire on my words. Long for them, and you princes will be instructed. 12 Wisdom11 is radiant and doesn’t fade away; and is easily seen by those who love12 her, and found by those who seek her. 13 She anticipates those who desire her, making herself known. 14 He who rises up early to seek her won’t have difficulty, for he will find her sitting at his gates. 15 For to think upon her is perfection of understanding, and he who watches for her will quickly be free from care;13 16 because she herself goes around, seeking those who are worthy of her, and in their paths she appears to them graciously, and in every purpose she meets them. 17 For her true beginning is desire for instruction; and desire for instruction is love14. 18 And love15 is observance of her laws. To give heed to her laws confirms immortality. 19 Immortality brings closeness to God16. 20 So then desire for wisdom17 promotes to a kingdom. 21 If therefore you delight in thrones and sceptres, you princes of peoples, honor wisdom18, that you may reign forever. 22 But what wisdom19 is, and how she came into being, I will declare. I won’t hide mysteries from you; but I will explore from her first beginning, bring the knowledge of her into clear light20, and I will not pass by the truth. 23 Indeed, I won’t travel with consuming envy, because envy will have no fellowship with wisdom21.22 24 But a multitude of wise men is salvation to the world, and an understanding king is stability for his people. 25 Therefore be instructed by my words, and you will profit.

23

7

1 I myself am also mortal, like everyone else, and am a descendant of one formed first and born of the earth1.2 2 I molded into flesh in the time of ten months in my mother’s womb, being compacted in blood3 from the seed of man4 and pleasure of marriage. 3 I also, when I was born, drew in the common air, and fell upon the kindred earth5, uttering, like all, for my first voice, the same cry. 4 I was nursed with care in swaddling clothes. 5 For no king had a different beginning, 6 but all men have one entrance into life, and a common departure. 7 For this cause I prayed, and understanding was given to me. I asked, and a spirit6 of wisdom7 came to me.8 8 I preferred her before sceptres and thrones. I considered riches nothing in comparison to her. 9 Neither did I liken to her any priceless gem, because all gold in her presence is a little sand, and silver will be considered as clay before her. 10 I loved her more than health and beauty, and I chose to have her rather than light9, because her bright shining is never laid to sleep. 11 All good10 things came to me with her, and innumerable riches are in her hands. 12 And I rejoiced over them all because wisdom11 leads them; although I didn’t know that she was their mother. 13 As I learned without guile, I impart without grudging. I don’t hide her riches. 14 For she is a treasure for men that doesn’t fail, and those who use it obtain friendship with God12, commended by the gifts which they present through discipline. 15 But may God13 grant that I may speak his judgment, and to conceive thoughts worthy of what has been given me; because he is one who guides even wisdom14 and who corrects the wise. 16 For both we and our words are in his hand, with all understanding and skill in various crafts.15 17 For he himself gave me an unerring knowledge of the things that are, to know the structure of the universe and the operation of the elements; 18 the beginning, end, and middle of times; the alternations of the solstices and the changes of seasons; 19 the circuits of years and the positions of stars; 20 the natures of living creatures and the raging of wild beasts; the violence of winds and the thoughts of men; the diversities of plants and the virtues of roots. 21 All things that are either secret or manifest I learned, 22 for wisdom16, that is the architect of all things, taught me. For there is in her a spirit17 that is quick to understand, holy18, unique, manifold, subtle, freely moving, clear in utterance, unpolluted, distinct, invulnerable, loving what is good19, keen, unhindered, 23 beneficent, loving toward man20, steadfast, sure, free from care, all-powerful, all-surveying, and penetrating through all spirits that are quick to understand, pure, most subtle. 24 For wisdom21 is more mobile than any motion. Yes, she pervades and penetrates all things by reason of her purity. 25 For she is a breath22 of the power of God23, and a pure emanation of the glory24 of the Almighty. Therefore nothing defiled can find entrance into her. 26 For she is a reflection of everlasting light25, an unspotted mirror of the working of God26, and an image27 of his goodness. 27 Although she is one, she has power to do all things. Remaining in herself, she renews all things. From generation to generation passing into holy28 souls, she makes friends of God29 and prophets. 28 For God30 loves nothing as much as one who dwells with wisdom31. 29 For she is fairer than the sun, and above all the constellations of the stars. She is better than light32. 30 For daylight yields to night, but evil does not prevail against wisdom33.

8

1 But she reaches from one end to the other with full strength, and orders all things well.1 2 I loved her and sought her from my youth. I sought to take her for my bride. I became enamoured by her beauty. 3 She glorifies her noble birth by living with God2. The Sovereign Lord3 of all loves her. 4 For she is initiated into the knowledge of God4, and she chooses his works. 5 But if riches are a desired possession in life, what is richer than wisdom5, which makes all things? 6 And if understanding is effective, who more than wisdom is an architect of the things that exist? 7 If a man6 love7s righteousness8, the fruits of wisdom’s labor are virtues, for she teaches soberness, understanding, righteousness, and courage. There is nothing in life more profitable for people than these. 8 And if anyone longs for wide experience, she knows the things of old, and infers the things to come. She understands subtleties of speeches and interpretations of dark sayings. She foresees signs and wonders, and the issues of seasons and times.9 9 Therefore I determined to take her to live with me, knowing that she is one who would give me good10 counsel, and encourage me in cares and grief. 10 Because of her, I will have glory among multitudes, and honor in the sight of elders, though I am young. 11 I will be found keen when I give judgment. I will be admired in the presence of rulers. 12 When I am silent, they will wait for me. When I open my lips, they will heed what I say. If I continue speaking, they will put their hands on their mouths.11 13 Because of her, I will have immortality, and leave behind an eternal memory to those who come after me. 14 I will govern peoples. Nations will be subjected to me. 15 Dreaded monarchs will fear me when they hear of me. Among the people, I will show myself to be good12, and courageous in war. 16 When I come into my house, I will find rest with her. For conversation with her has no bitterness, and living with her has no pain, but gladness and joy. 17 When I considered these things in myself, and thought in my heart13 how immortality is in kinship to wisdom14, 18 and in her friendship is good15 delight, and in the labors of her hands is wealth that doesn’t fail, and understanding is in her companionship, and great renown in having fellowship with her words, I went about seeking how to take her to myself. 19 Now I was a clever child, and received a good16 soul.17 20 Or rather, being good18, I came into an undefiled body. 21 But perceiving that I could not otherwise possess wisdom19 unless God20 gave her to me— yes, and to know and understand by whom the grace is given— I pleaded with the Lord21 and implored him, and with my whole heart22 I said: 9

1 “O God1 of my ancestors and Lord2 of mercy3, who made all things by your word; 2 and by your wisdom4 you formed man5, that he should have dominion over the creatures that were made by you, 3 and rule the world in holiness and righteousness6, and execute judgment in uprightness of soul,7 4 give me wisdom8, her who sits by you on your thrones. Don’t reject me from among your servants, 5 because I am your servant and the son of your handmaid, a weak and short-lived man, with little power to understand judgment and laws. 6 For even if a man9 is perfect among the sons of men, if the wisdom10 that comes from you is not with him, he will count for nothing. 7 You chose me to be king of your people, and a judge for your sons and daughters. 8 You gave a command to build a sanctuary on your holy11 mountain, and an altar in the city where you live, a copy of the holy tent which you prepared from the beginning. 9 Wisdom is with you and knows your works, and was present when you were making the world, and understands what is pleasing in your eyes, and what is right according to your commandments.12 10 Send her from the holy13 heavens14, and ask her to come from the throne of your glory15, that being present with me she may work, and I may learn what pleases you well. 11 For she knows all things and understands, and she will guide me prudently in my actions. She will guard me in her glory. 12 So my works will be acceptible. I will judge your people righteously, and I will be worthy of my father’s throne. 13 For what man16 will know the counsel of God17? Or who will conceive what the Lord18 wills? 14 For the thoughts of mortals are unstable, and our plans are prone to fail. 15 For a corruptible body weighs down the soul19. The earthy tent burdens a mind that is full of cares. 16 We can hardly guess the things that are on earth20, and we find the things that are close at hand with labor; but who has traced out the things that are in the heaven21s? 17 Who gained knowledge of your counsel, unless you gave wisdom22, and sent your holy spirit from on high?2324 18 It was thus that the ways of those who are on earth25 were corrected, and men were taught the things that are pleasing to you. They were saved through wisdom26.”

10

1 Wisdom guarded to the end the first formed father of the world, who was created1 alone, and delivered him out of his own transgression, 2 and gave him strength to rule over all things. 3 But when an unrighteous man fell away from her in his anger, he perished himself in the rage with which he killed his brother. 4 When for his cause the earth2 was drowning with a flood, wisdom3 again saved it, guiding the righteous4 man’s course by a paltry piece of wood. 5 Moreover, when nations consenting together in wickedness had been confounded, wisdom knew the righteous5 man, and preserved him blameless to God6, and kept him strong when his heart yearned toward his child. 6 While the ungodly were perishing, wisdom delivered a righteous7 man8, when he fled from the fire that descended out of heaven on the five cities. 7 To whose wickedness a smoking waste9 still witnesses, and plants bearing fair fruit that doesn’t ripen, a disbelieving soul10 has a memorial: a standing pillar of salt.11 8 For having passed wisdom12 by, not only were they disabled from recognising the things which are good13, but they also left behind them for their life a monument of their folly, to the end that where they stumbled, they might fail even to be unseen; 9 but wisdom14 delivered those who waited on her out of troubles. 10 When a righteous15 man was a fugitive from a brother’s wrath, wisdom guided him in straight paths. She showed him God16’s kingdom, and gave him knowledge of holy17 things. She prospered him in his toils, and multiplied the fruits of his labor. 11 When in their covetousness men dealt harshly with him, she stood by him and made him rich. 12 She guarded him from enemies, and she kept him safe from those who lay in wait. Over his severe conflict, she watched as judge, that he might know that godliness is more powerful than every one. 13 When a righteous18 man was sold, wisdom didn’t forsake him, but she delivered him from sin19. She went down with him into a dungeon, 14 and in bonds she didn’t depart from him, until she brought him the sceptre of a kingdom, and authority over those that dealt like a tyrant with him. She also showed those who had mockingly accused him to be false, and gave him eternal glory20. 15 Wisdom delivered a holy people and a blameless seed from a nation of oppressors.21 16 She entered into the soul22 of a servant of the Lord23, and withstood terrible kings in wonders and signs. 17 She rendered to holy men a reward of their toils. She guided them along a marvelous way, and became to them a covering in the day-time, and a starry flame through the night.2425 18 She brought them over the Red sea, and led them through much water26; 19 but she drowned their enemies, and she cast them up from the bottom of the deep27. 20 Therefore the righteous28 plundered the ungodly, and they sang praise to your holy29 name, O Lord30, and extolled with one accord your hand that fought for them, 21 because wisdom31 opened the mouth of the mute, and made the tongues of babes to speak clearly.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). THORN (1.) Hebrews hedek (Proverbs 15:19), rendered “brier” in Micah 7:4. Some thorny plant, of the Solanum family, suitable for hedges. This is probably the so-called “apple of Sodom,” which grows very abundantly in the Jordan valley. “It is a shrubby plant, from 3 to 5 feet high, with very branching stems, thickly clad with spines, like those of the English brier, with leaves very large and woolly on the under side, and thorny on the midriff.” (2.) Hebrews kotz (Genesis 3:18; Hos. 10:8), rendered akantha by the LXX. In the New Testament this word akantha is also rendered “thorns” (Matthew 7:16; 13:7; Hebrews 6:8). The word seems to denote any thorny or prickly plant (Jeremiah 12:13). It has been identified with the Ononis spinosa by some. (3.) Hebrews na’atzutz (Isaiah 7:19; 55:13). This word has been interpreted as denoting the Zizyphus spina Christi, or the jujube-tree. It is supposed by some that the crown of thorns placed in wanton cruelty by the Roman soldiers on our Saviour’s brow before his crucifixion was plaited of branches of this tree. It overruns a great part of the Jordan valley. It is sometimes called the lotus-tree. “The thorns are long and sharp and recurved, and often create a festering wound.” It often grows to a great size. (See CROWN OF THORNS.) (4.) Hebrews atad (Psalm 58:9) is rendered in the LXX. and Vulgate by Rhamnus, or Lycium Europoeum, a thorny shrub, which is common all over Palestine. From its resemblance to the box it is frequently called the box-thorn.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). GIFT (1.) An gratuity (Proverbs 19:6) to secure favour (18:16; 21:14), a thank-offering (Numbers 18:11), or a dowry (Genesis 34:12). (2.) An oblation or proppitatory gift (2Sa 8:2,6; 1Ch 18:2,6; 2Ch 26:8; Psalm 45:12; 72:10). (3.) A bribe to a judge to obtain a favourable verdict (Exodus 23:8; Deuteronomy 16:19). (4.) Simply a thing given (Matthew 7:11; Luke 11:13; Ephesians 4:8); sacrifical (Matthew 5:23, 24; 8:4); eleemosynary (Luke 21:1); a gratuity (John 4:10; Acts 8:20). In Acts 2:38 the generic word dorea is rendered “gift.” It differs from the charisma (1 Corinthians 12:4) as denoting not miraculous powers but the working of a new spirit in men, and that spirit from God. The giving of presents entered largely into the affairs of common life in the East. The nature of the presents was as various as were the occasions: food (1 Samuel 9:7; 16:20), sheep and cattle (Genesis 32:13-15), gold (2 Samuel 18:11), jewels (Genesis 24:53), furniture, and vessels for eating and drinking (2 Samuel 17:28); delicacies, as spices, honey, etc. (1 Kings 10:25; 2 Kings 5: 22). The mode of presentation was with as much parade as possible: the presents were conveyed by the hands of servants (Judges 3:18), or still better, on the backs of beasts of burden (2 Kings 8:9). The refusal of a present was regarded as a high indignity; and this constituted the aggravated insult noticed in Matthew 22:11, the marriage robe having been offered and refused.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NETTLE (1.) Hebrews haral, “pricking” or “burning,” Proverbs 24:30, 31 (R.V. marg., “wild vetches”); Job 30:7; Zephaniah 2:9. Many have supposed that some thorny or prickly plant is intended by this word, such as the bramble, the thistle, the wild plum, the cactus or prickly pear, etc. It may probably be a species of mustard, the Sinapis arvensis, which is a pernicious weed abounding in corn-fields. Tristram thinks that this word “designates the prickly acanthus (Acanthus spinosus), a very common and troublesome weed in the plains of Palestine.” (2.) Hebrews qimmosh, Isaiah 34:13; Hos. 9:6; Proverbs 24:31 (in both versions, “thorns”). This word has been regarded as denoting thorns, thistles, wild camomile; but probably it is correctly rendered “nettle,” the Urtica pilulifera, “a tall and vigorous plant, often 6 feet high, the sting of which is much more severe and irritating than that of our common nettle.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). FULLER’S SOAP (Hebrews borith mekabbeshim, i.e., “alkali of those treading cloth”). Mention is made (Proverbs 25:20; Jeremiah 2:22) of nitre and also (Malachi 3:2) of soap (Hebrews borith) used by the fuller in his operations. Nitre is found in Syria, and vegetable alkali was obtained from the ashes of certain plants. (See SOAP.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). NITRE (Proverbs 25:20; R.V. marg., “soda”), properly “natron,” a substance so called because, rising from the bottom of the Lake Natron in Egypt, it becomes dry and hard in the sun, and is the soda which effervesces when vinegar is poured on it. It is a carbonate of soda, not saltpetre, which the word generally denotes (Jeremiah 2:22; R.V. “lye”).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). DOORS moved on pivots of wood fastened in sockets above and below (Proverbs 26:14). They were fastened by a lock (Judges 3:23, 25; Cant. 5:5) or by a bar (Judges 16:3; Job 38:10). In the interior of Oriental houses, curtains were frequently used instead of doors. The entrances of the tabernacle had curtains (Exodus 26:31-33, 36). The “valley of Achor” is called a “door of hope,” because immediately after the execution of Achan the Lord said to Joshua, “Fear not,” and from that time Joshua went forward in a career of uninterrupted conquest. Paul speaks of a “door opened” for the spread of the gospel (1 Corinthians 16:9; 2 Corinthians 2:12; Colossians 4:3). Our Lord says of himself, “I am the door” (John 10:9). John (Revelation 4:1) speaks of a “door opened in heaven.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HINGE (Hebrews tsir), that on which a door revolves. “Doors in the East turn rather on pivots than on what we term hinges. In Syria, and especially in the Hauran, there are many ancient doors, consisting of stone slabs with pivots carved out of the same piece inserted in sockets above and below, and fixed during the building of the house” (Proverbs 26:14).

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). COAL It is by no means certain that the Hebrews were acquainted with mineral coal, although it is found in Syria. Their common fuel was dried dung of animals and wood charcoal. Two different words are found in Hebrew to denote coal, both occurring in Proverbs 26:21, “As coal [Hebrews peham; i.e., “black coal”] is to burning coal [Hebrews gehalim].” The latter of these words is used in Job 41:21; Proverbs 6:28; Isaiah 44:19. The words “live coal” in Isaiah 6:6 are more correctly “glowing stone.” In Lamentations 4:8 the expression “blacker than a coal” is literally rendered in the margin of the Revised Version “darker than blackness.” “Coals of fire” (2 Samuel 22:9, 13; Psalm 18:8, 12, 13, etc.) is an expression used metaphorically for lightnings proceeding from God. A false tongue is compared to “coals of juniper” (Psalm 120:4; James 3:6). “Heaping coals of fire on the head” symbolizes overcoming evil with good. The words of Paul (Romans 12:20) are equivalent to saying, “By charity and kindness thou shalt soften down his enmity as surely as heaping coals on the fire fuses the metal in the crucible.”

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HELL derived from the Saxon helan, to cover; hence the covered or the invisible place. In Scripture there are three words so rendered: (1.) Sheol, occurring in the Old Testament sixty-five times. This word sheol is derived from a root-word meaning “to ask,” “demand;” hence insatiableness (Proverbs 30:15, 16). It is rendered “grave” thirty-one times (Genesis 37:35; 42:38; 44:29, 31; 1 Samuel 2:6, etc.). The Revisers have retained this rendering in the historical books with the original word in the margin, while in the poetical books they have reversed this rule. In thirty-one cases in the Authorized Version this word is rendered “hell,” the place of disembodied spirits. The inhabitants of sheol are “the congregation of the dead” (Proverbs 21:16). It is (a) the abode of the wicked (Numbers 16:33; Job 24:19; Psalm 9:17; 31:17, etc.); (b) of the good (Psalm 16:10; 30:3; 49:15; 86:13, etc.). Sheol is described as deep (Job 11:8), dark (10:21, 22), with bars (17:16). The dead “go down” to it (Numbers 16:30, 33; Ezekiel 31:15, 16, 17). (2.) The Greek word hades of the New Testament has the same scope of signification as sheol of the Old Testament. It is a prison (1 Peter 3:19), with gates and bars and locks (Matthew 16:18; Revelation 1:18), and it is downward (Matthew 11:23; Luke 10:15). The righteous and the wicked are separated. The blessed dead are in that part of hades called paradise (Luke 23:43). They are also said to be in Abraham’s bosom (Luke 16:22). (3.) Gehenna, in most of its occurrences in the Greek New Testament, designates the place of the lost (Matthew 23:33). The fearful nature of their condition there is described in various figurative expressions (Matthew 8:12; 13:42; 22:13; 25:30; Luke 16:24, etc.). (See HINNOM.)

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). HORSE-LEECH occurs only in Proverbs 30:15 (Hebrews ‘alukah); the generic name for any blood-sucking annelid. There are various species in the marshes and pools of Palestine. That here referred to, the Hoemopis, is remarkable for the coarseness of its bite, and is therefore not used for medical purposes. They are spoken of in the East with feelings of aversion and horror, because of their propensity to fasten on the tongue and nostrils of horses when they come to drink out of the pools. The medicinal leech (Hirudo medicinalis), besides other species of leeches, are common in the waters of Syria.

↩ ⌂ Easton. Dictionary (Easton's). CONEY (Hebrews shaphan; i.e., “the hider”), an animal which inhabits the mountain gorges and the rocky districts of Arabia Petraea and the Holy Land. “The conies are but a feeble folk, yet make they their houses in the rocks” (Proverbs 30:26; Psalm 104:18). They are gregarious, and “exceeding wise” (Proverbs 30:24), and are described as chewing the cud (Leviticus 11:5; Deuteronomy 14:7). The animal intended by this name is known among naturalists as the Hyrax Syriacus. It is neither a ruminant nor a rodent, but is regarded as akin to the rhinoceros. When it is said to “chew the cud,” the Hebrew word so used does not necessarily imply the possession of a ruminant stomach. “The lawgiver speaks according to appearances; and no one can watch the constant motion of the little creature’s jaws, as it sits continually working its teeth, without recognizing the naturalness of the expression” (Tristram, Natural History of the Bible). It is about the size and color of a rabbit, though clumsier in structure, and without a tail. Its feet are not formed for digging, and therefore it has its home not in burrows but in the clefts of the rocks. “Coney” is an obsolete English word for “rabbit.”

GREYHOUND (Proverbs 30:31), the rendering of the Hebrew zarzir mothnayim, meaning literally “girded as to the lions.” Some (Gesen.; R.V. marg.) render it “war-horse.” The LXX. and Vulgate versions render it “cock.” It has been by some interpreters rendered also “stag” and “warrior,” as being girded about or panoplied, and “wrestler.” The greyhound, however, was evidently known in ancient times, as appears from Egyptian monuments.

The Proverbs 10:1.

The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father: but a foolish son [is] the heaviness of his mother.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

מִשְׁלֵ֗י שְׁלֹ֫מֹ֥ה בֵּ֣ן חָ֭כָם יְשַׂמַּח־אָ֑ב וּבֵ֥ן כְּ֝סִ֗יל תּוּגַ֥ת אִמּֽוֹ׃

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Υἱὸς σοφὸς εὐφραίνει πατέρα, υἱὸς δὲ ἄφρων λύπη τῇ μητρί.

Douay-Rheims

A wise son maketh the father glad: but a foolish son is the sorrow of his mother.

JPS (1917)

The proverbs of Solomon. A wise son maketh a glad father; but a foolish son is the grief of his mother.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

[Filius sapiens lætificat patrem, filius vero stultus mœstitia est matris suæ.

Arabic (Van Dyck)

أَمْثَالُ سُلَيْمَانَ: اَلِٱبْنُ ٱلْحَكِيمُ يَسُرُّ أَبَاهُ، وَٱلِٱبْنُ ٱلْجَاهِلُ حُزْنُ أُمِّهِ.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

Treasures of wickedness profit nothing; but righteousness delivereth from death.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

JPS (1917)

The Proverbs 10:4.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

The Proverbs 10:5.

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

אֹגֵ֣ר בַּ֭קַּיִץ בֵּ֣ן מַשְׂכִּ֑יל נִרְדָּ֥ם בַּ֝קָּצִ֗יר בֵּ֣ן מֵבִֽישׁ׃

JPS (1917)

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Hebrew (Masoretic / WLC)

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

τίς ἀνέβη εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν καὶ κατέβη; τίς συνήγαγεν ἀνέμους ἐν κόλπῳ; τίς συνέστρεψεν ὕδωρ ἐν ἱματίῳ; τίς ἐκράτησεν τῶν ἄκρων τῆς γῆς, τί ὄνομα αὐτῷ; ἢ τί ὄνομα τοῖς τέκνοις αὐτοῦ;

Douay-Rheims

JPS (1917)

Let us fill ourselves with costly wine and ointments: and let no flower of the spring pass by us:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

οἴνου πολυτελοῦς καὶ μύρων πλησθῶμεν, καὶ μὴ παροδευσάτω ἡμᾶς ἄνθος ἀέρος·

Douay-Rheims

Let us fill ourselves with costly wine, and ointments: and let not the flower of the time pass by us.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Vino pretioso et unguentis nos impleamus, et non prætereat nos flos temporis.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:8.

Let us crown ourselves with rosebuds, before they be withered:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

στεψώμεθα ῥόδων κάλυξιν πρὶν ἢ μαρανθῆναι·

Douay-Rheims

Let us crown ourselves with roses, before they be withered: let no meadow escape our riot.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Coronemus nos rosis antequam marcescant; nullum pratum sit quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra:

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:9.

Let none of us go without his part of our voluptuousness: let us leave tokens of our joyfulness in every place: for this is our portion, and our lot is this.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

μηδεὶς ἡμῶν ἄμοιρος ἔστω τῆς ἡμετέρας ἀγερωχίας, πανταχῇ καταλίπωμεν σύμβολα τῆς εὐφροσύνης, ὅτι αὕτη ἡ μερὶς ἡμῶν καὶ ὁ κλῆρος οὗτος.

Douay-Rheims

Let none of us go without his part in luxury: let us everywhere leave tokens of joy: for this is our portion, and this our lot.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

nemo nostrum exsors sit luxuriæ nostræ. Ubique relinquamus signa lætitiæ, quoniam hæc est pars nostra, et hæc est sors.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:10.

Let us oppress the poor righteous man, let us not spare the widow, nor reverence the ancient gray hairs of the aged.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καταδυναστεύσωμεν πένητα δίκαιον, μὴ φεισώμεθα χήρας, μηδὲ πρεσβύτου ἐντραπῶμεν πολιὰς πολυχρονίους·

Douay-Rheims

Let us oppress the poor just man, and not spare the widow, nor honour the ancient grey hairs of the aged.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Opprimamus pauperem justum, et non parcamus viduæ, nec veterani revereamur canos multi temporis:

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:11.

Let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble is found to be nothing worth.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἔστω δὲ ἡμῶν ἡ ἰσχὺς νόμος τῆς δικαιοσύνης, τὸ γὰρ ἀσθενὲς ἄχρηστον ἐλέγχεται.

Douay-Rheims

But let our strength be the law of justice: for that which is feeble, is found to be nothing worth.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

sit autem fortitudo nostra lex justitiæ; quod enim infirmum est, inutile invenitur.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:12.

Therefore let us lie in wait for the righteous; because he is not for our turn, and he is clean contrary to our doings: he upbraideth us with our offending the law, and objecteth to our infamy the transgressings of our education.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐνεδρεύσωμεν δὲ τὸν δίκαιον, ὅτι δύσχρηστος ἡμῖν ἐστιν, καὶ ἐναντιοῦται τοῖς ἔργοις ἡμῶν, καὶ ὀνειδίζει ἡμῖν ἁμαρτήματα νόμου, καὶ ἐπιφημίζει ἡμῖν ἁμαρτήματα παιδείας ἡμῶν·

Douay-Rheims

Let us therefore lie in wait for the just, because he is not for our turn, and he is contrary to our doings, and upbraideth us with transgressions of the law, and divulgeth against us the sins of our way of life.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Circumveniamus ergo justum, quoniam inutilis est nobis, et contrarius est operibus nostris, et improperat nobis peccata legis, et diffamat in nos peccata disciplinæ nostræ.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:13.

He professeth to have the knowledge of God: and he calleth himself the child of the Lord.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐπαγγέλλεται γνῶσιν ἔχειν θεοῦ, καὶ παῖδα Κυρίου ἑαυτὸν ὀνομάζει·

Douay-Rheims

He boasteth that he hath the knowledge of God, and calleth himself the son of God.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Promittit se scientiam Dei habere, et filium Dei se nominat.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:14.

He was made to reprove our thoughts.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐγένετο ἡμῖν εἰς ἔλεγχον ἐννοιῶν ἡμῶν· βαρύς ἐστιν ἡμῖν καὶ βλεπόμενος,

Douay-Rheims

He is become a censurer of our thoughts.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Factus est nobis in traductionem cogitationum nostrarum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:15.

He is grievous unto us even to behold: for his life is not like other men’s, his ways are of another fashion.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι ἀνόμοιος τοῖς ἄλλοις ὁ βίος αὐτοῦ, καὶ ἐξηλλαγμέναι αἱ τρίβοι αὐτοῦ·

Douay-Rheims

He is grievous unto us, even to behold: for his life is not like other men’s, and his ways are very different.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Gravis est nobis etiam ad videndum, quoniam dissimilis est aliis vita illius, et immutatæ sunt viæ ejus.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:16.

We are esteemed of him as counterfeits: he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness: he pronounceth the end of the just to be blessed, and maketh his boast that God is his father.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

εἰς κίβδηλον ἐλογίσθημεν αὐτῷ, καὶ ἀπέχεται τῶν ὁδῶν ἡμῶν ὡς ἀπὸ ἀκαθαρσιῶν· μακαρίζει ἔσχατα δικαίων, καὶ ἀλαζονεύεται πατέρα θεόν.

Douay-Rheims

We are esteemed by him as triflers, and he abstaineth from our ways as from filthiness, and he preferreth the latter end of the just, and glorieth that he hath God for his father.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Tamquam nugaces æstimati sumus ab illo, et abstinet se a viis nostris tamquam ab immunditiis, et præfert novissima justorum, et gloriatur patrem se habere Deum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:17.

Let us see if his words be true: and let us prove what shall happen in the end of him.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἴδωμεν εἰ οἱ λόγοι αὐτοῦ ἀληθεῖς, καὶ πειράσωμεν τὰ ἐν ἐκβάσει αὐτοῦ.

Douay-Rheims

Let us see then if his words be true, and let us prove what shall happen to him, and we shall know what his end shall be.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Videamus ergo si sermones illius veri sint, et tentemus quæ ventura sunt illi, et sciemus quæ erunt novissima illius.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:18.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

εἰ γάρ ἐστιν ὁ δίκαιος υἱὸς θεοῦ, ἀντιλήμψεται αὐτοῦ, καὶ ῥύσεται αὐτὸν ἐκ χειρὸς ἀνθεστηκότων.

Douay-Rheims

For if he be the true son of God, he will defend him, and will deliver him from the hands of his enemies.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Si enim est verus filius Dei, suscipiet illum, et liberabit eum de manibus contrariorum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:19.

Let us examine him with despitefulness and torture, that we may know his meekness, and prove his patience.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὕβρει καὶ βασάνῳ ἐτάσωμεν αὐτόν, ἵνα γνῶμεν τὴν ἐπιεικίαν αὐτοῦ καὶ δικάσωμεν τὴν ἀνεξικακίαν αὐτοῦ·

Douay-Rheims

Let us examine him by outrages and tortures, that we may know his meekness and try his patience.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Contumelia et tormento interrogemus eum, ut sciamus reverentiam ejus, et probemus patientiam illius.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:20.

Let us condemn him with a shameful death: for by his own saying he shall be respected.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

θανάτῳ ἀσχήμονι καταδικάσωμεν αὐτόν, ἔσται γὰρ αὐτοῦ ἐπισκοπὴ ἐκ λόγων αὐτοῦ.

Douay-Rheims

Let us condemn him to a most shameful death: for there shall be respect had unto him by his words.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Morte turpissima condemnemus eum; erit enim ei respectus ex sermonibus illius.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:21.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ταῦτα ἐλογίσαντο, καὶ ἐπλανήθησαν· ἀπετύφλωσεν γὰρ αὐτοὺς ἡ κακία αὐτῶν,

Douay-Rheims

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:22.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ οὐκ ἔγνωσαν μυστήρια αὐτοῦ, οὐδὲ μισθὸν ἤλπισαν ὁσιότητος, οὐδὲ ἔκριναν γέρας ψυχῶν ἀμώμων.

Douay-Rheims

And they knew not the secrets of God, nor hoped for the wages of justice, nor esteemed the honour of holy souls.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:23.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι ὁ θεὸς ἔκτισεν τὸν ἄνθρωπον ἐπ᾽ ἀφθαρσίᾳ, καὶ εἰκόνα τῆς ἰδίας ἰδιότητος ἐποίησεν αὐτόν·

Douay-Rheims

For God created man incorruptible, and to the image of his own likeness he made him.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 2:24.

Douay-Rheims

But by the envy of the devil, death came into the world: And they follow him that are of his side.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Invidia autem diaboli mors introivit in orbem terrarum: imitantur autem illum qui sunt ex parte illius.]

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 3:1.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

[Justorum autem animæ in manu Dei sunt, et non tangent illos tormentum mortis.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 3:2.

Douay-Rheims

In the sight of the unwise they seemed to die: and their departure was taken for misery:

Visi sunt oculis insipientium mori, et æstimata est afflictio exitus illorum,

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 3:3.

Douay-Rheims

↩

↩

↩

Douay-Rheims

They shall judge nations, and rule over people, and their Lord shall reign for ever.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

↩

Douay-Rheims

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 3:10.

Douay-Rheims

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Douay-Rheims

Douay-Rheims

↩

Maledicta creatura eorum, quoniam felix est sterilis; et incoinquinata, quæ nescivit thorum in delicto, habebit fructum in respectione animarum sanctarum;

↩

et spado qui non operatus est per manus suas iniquitatem, nec cogitavit adversus Deum nequissima: dabitur enim illi fidei donum electum, et sors in templo Dei acceptissima.

↩

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 3:19.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

↩

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:3.

πολύγονον δὲ ἀσεβῶν πλῆθος οὐ χρησιμεύσει, καὶ ἐκ νόθων μοσχευμάτων οὐ δώσει ῥίζαν εἰς βάθος, οὐδὲ ἀσφαλῆ βάσιν ἑδράσει·

Douay-Rheims

But the multiplied brood of the wicked shall not thrive, and bastard slips shall not take deep root, nor any fast foundation.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Multigena autem impiorum multitudo non erit utilis, et spuria vitulamina non dabunt radices altas, nec stabile firmamentum collocabunt.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:4.

For though they flourish in branches for a time; yet standing not last, they shall be shaken with the wind, and through the force of winds they shall be rooted out.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

κἂν γὰρ ἐν κλάδοις πρὸς καιρὸν ἀναθάλῃ, ἐπισφαλῶς βεβηκότα ὑπὸ ἀνέμου σαλευθήσεται, καὶ ὑπὸ βίας ἀνέμων ἐκριζωθήσεται·

Douay-Rheims

And if they flourish in branches for a time, yet standing not fast, they shall be shaken with the wind, and through the force of winds they shall be rooted out.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Etsi in ramis in tempore germinaverint, infirmiter posita, a vento commovebuntur, et a nimietate ventorum eradicabuntur.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:5.

The imperfect branches shall be broken off, their fruit unprofitable, not ripe to eat, yea, meet for nothing.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

περικλασθήσονται κλῶνες ἀτέλεστοι, καὶ ὁ καρπὸς αὐτῶν ἄχρηστος, ἄωρος εἰς βρῶσιν καὶ εἰς οὐθὲν ἐπιτήδειος·

Douay-Rheims

For the branches not being perfect, shall be broken, and their fruits shall be unprofitable, and sour to eat, and fit for nothing.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Confringentur enim rami inconsummati; et fructus illorum inutiles et acerbi ad manducandum, et ad nihilum apti.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:6.

For children begotten of unlawful beds are witnesses of wickedness against their parents in their trial.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐκ γὰρ ἀνόμων ὕπνων τέκνα γεννώμενα μάρτυρές εἰσιν πονηρίας κατὰ γονέων ἐν ἐξετασμῷ αὐτῶν·

Douay-Rheims

For the children that are born of unlawful beds, are witnesses of wickedness against their parents in their trial.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ex iniquis enim somnis filii qui nascuntur, testes sunt nequitiæ adversus parentes in interrogatione sua.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:7.

But though the righteous be prevented with death, yet shall he be in rest.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

δίκαιος δὲ ἐὰν φθάσῃ τελευτῆσαι, ἐν ἀναπαύσει ἔσται.

Douay-Rheims

But the just man, if he be prevented with death, shall be in rest.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Justus autem si morte præoccupatus fuerit, in refrigerio erit;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:8.

For honourable age is not that which standeth in length of time, nor that is measured by number of years.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

γῆρας γὰρ τίμιον οὐ τὸ πολυχρόνιον, οὐδὲ ἀριθμῷ ἐτῶν μεμέτρηται·

Douay-Rheims

For venerable old age is not that of long time, nor counted by the number of years: but the understanding of a man is grey hairs.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

senectus enim venerabilis est non diuturna, neque annorum numero computata: cani autem sunt sensus hominis,

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:9.

But wisdom is the gray hair unto men, and an unspotted life is old age.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

πολιὰ δέ ἐστιν φρόνησις ἀνθρώποις, καὶ ἡλικία γήρως βίος ἀκηλίδωτος.

Douay-Rheims

And a spotless life is old age.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

et ætas senectutis vita immaculata.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:10.

He pleased God, and was beloved of him: so that living among sinners he was translated.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

εὐάρεστος τῷ θεῷ γενόμενος ἠγαπήθη, καὶ ζῶν μεταξὺ ἁμαρτωλῶν μετετέθη·

Douay-Rheims

He pleased God and was beloved, and living among sinners he was translated.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Placens Deo factus est dilectus, et vivens inter peccatores translatus est.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:11.

Yea speedily was he taken away, lest that wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἡρπάγη, μὴ κακία ἀλλάξῃ σύνεσιν αὐτοῦ, ἢ δόλος ἀπατήσῃ ψυχὴν αὐτοῦ·

Douay-Rheims

He was taken away lest wickedness should alter his understanding, or deceit beguile his soul.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Raptus est, ne malitia mutaret intellectum ejus, aut ne fictio deciperet animam illius.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:12.

For the bewitching of naughtiness doth obscure things that are honest; and the wandering of concupiscence doth undermine the simple mind.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

βασκανία γὰρ φαυλότητος ἀμαυροῖ τὰ καλά, καὶ ῥεμβασμὸς ἐπιθυμίας μεταλλεύει νοῦν ἄκακον.

Douay-Rheims

For the bewitching of vanity obscureth good things, and the wandering of concupiscence overturneth the innocent mind.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Fascinatio enim nugacitatis obscurat bona, et inconstantia concupiscentiæ transvertit sensum sine malitia.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:13.

He, being made perfect in a short time, fulfilled a long time:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

τελειωθεὶς ἐν ὀλίγῳ ἐπλήρωσεν χρόνους μακρούς·

Douay-Rheims

Being made perfect in a short space, he fulfilled a long time:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Consummatus in brevi, explevit tempora multa;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:14.

For his soul pleased the Lord: therefore hasted he to take him away from among the wicked.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἀρεστὴ γὰρ ἦν Κυρίῳ ἡ ψυχὴ αὐτοῦ, διὰ τοῦτο ἔσπευσεν ἐκ μέσου πονηρίας· οἱ δὲ λαοὶ ἰδόντες καὶ μὴ νοήσαντες, μηδὲ θέντες ἐπὶ διανοίᾳ τὸ τοιοῦτο,

Douay-Rheims

For his soul pleased God: therefore he hastened to bring him out of the midst of iniquities: but the people see this, and understand not, nor lay up such things in their hearts:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

placita enim erat Deo anima illius: propter hoc properavit educere illum de medio iniquitatum. Populi autem videntes, et non intelligentes, nec ponentes in præcordiis talia,

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:15.

This the people saw, and understood it not, neither laid they up this in their minds, That his grace and mercy is with his saints, and that he hath respect unto his chosen.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι χάρις καὶ ἔλεος ἐν τοῖς ἐκλεκτοῖς αὐτοῦ καὶ ἐπισκοπὴ ἐν τοῖς ὁσίοις αὐτοῦ.

Douay-Rheims

That the grace of God, and his mercy is with his saints, and that he hath respect to his chosen.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

quoniam gratia Dei et misericordia est in sanctos ejus, et respectus in electos illius.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:16.

Thus the righteous that is dead shall condemn the ungodly which are living; and youth that is soon perfected the many years and old age of the unrighteous.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

κατακρινεῖ δὲ δίκαιος καμὼν τοὺς ζῶντας ἀσεβεῖς, καὶ νεότης τελεσθεῖσα ταχέως πολυετὲς γῆρας ἀδίκου.

Douay-Rheims

But the just that is dead, condemneth the wicked that are living, and youth soon ended, the long life of the unjust.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Condemnat autem justus mortuus vivos impios, et juventus celerius consummata longam vitam injusti.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:17.

For they shall see the end of the wise, and shall not understand what God in his counsel hath decreed of him, and to what end the Lord hath set him in safety.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὄψονται γὰρ τελευτὴν σοφοῦ, καὶ οὐ νοήσουσιν τί ἐβουλεύσατο περὶ αὐτοῦ, καὶ εἰς τί ἠσφαλίσατο αὐτὸν ὁ κύριος·

Douay-Rheims

For they shall see the end of the wise man, and shall not understand what God hath designed for him, and why the Lord hath set him in safety.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Videbunt enim finem sapientis, et non intelligent quid cogitaverit de illo Deus, et quare munierit illum Dominus.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:18.

They shall see him, and despise him; but God shall laugh them to scorn: and they shall hereafter be a vile carcase, and a reproach among the dead for evermore.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὄψονται καὶ ἐξουθενήσουσιν, αὐτοὺς δὲ ὁ κύριος ἐκγελάσεται·

Douay-Rheims

They shall see him, and shall despise him: but the Lord shall laugh them to scorn.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Videbunt, et contemnent eum; illos autem Dominus irridebit.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:19.

For he shall rend them, and cast them down headlong, that they shall be speechless; and he shall shake them from the foundation; and they shall be utterly laid waste, and be in sorrow; and their memorial shall perish.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

καὶ ἔσονται μετὰ τοῦτο εἰς πτῶμα ἄτιμον καὶ εἰς ὕβριν ἐν νεκροῖς δι᾽ αἰῶνος. ὅτι ῥήξει αὐτοὺς ἀφώνους πρηνεῖς, καὶ σαλεύσει αὐτοὺς ἐκ θεμελίων· καὶ ἕως ἐσχάτου χερσωθήσονται, καὶ ἔσονται ἐν ὀδύνῃ, καὶ ἡ μνήμη αὐτῶν ἀπολεῖται.

Douay-Rheims

And they shall fall after this without honour, and be a reproach among the dead for ever: for he shall burst them puffed up and speechless, and shall shake them from the foundations, and they shall be utterly laid waste: they shall be in sorrow, and their memory shall perish.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Et erunt post hæc decidentes sine honore, et in contumelia inter mortuos in perpetuum: quoniam disrumpet illos inflatos sine voce, et commovebit illos a fundamentis, et usque ad supremum desolabuntur, et erunt gementes, et memoria illorum peribit.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 4:20.

And when they cast up the accounts of their sins, they shall come with fear: and their own iniquities shall convince them to their face.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐλεύσονται ἐν συλλογισμῷ ἁμαρτημάτων αὐτῶν δειλοί, καὶ ἐλέγξει αὐτοὺς ἐξ ἐναντίας τὰ ἀνομήματα αὐτῶν.

Douay-Rheims

They shall come with fear at the thought of their sins, and their iniquities shall stand against them to convict them.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Venient in cogitatione peccatorum suorum timidi, et traducent illos ex adverso iniquitates ipsorum.]

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:1.

Then shall the righteous man stand in great boldness before the face of such as have afflicted him, and made no account of his labours.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

Τότε στήσεται ἐν παρρησίᾳ πολλῇ ὁ δίκαιος κατὰ πρόσωπον τῶν θλιψάντων αὐτὸν καὶ τῶν ἀθετούντων τοὺς πόνους αὐτοῦ.

Douay-Rheims

Then shall the just stand with great constancy against those that have afflicted them, and taken away their labours.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

[Tunc stabunt justi in magna constantia adversus eos qui se angustiaverunt, et qui abstulerunt labores eorum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:2.

When they see it, they shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall be amazed at the strangeness of his salvation, so far beyond all that they looked for.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἰδόντες ταραχθήσονται φόβῳ δεινῷ, καὶ ἐκστήσονται ἐπὶ τῷ παραδόξῳ τῆς σωτηρίας·

Douay-Rheims

These seeing it, shall be troubled with terrible fear, and shall be amazed at the suddenness of their unexpected salvation.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Videntes turbabuntur timore horribili, et mirabuntur in subitatione insperatæ salutis;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:3.

And they repenting and groaning for anguish of spirit shall say within themselves, This was he, whom we had sometimes in derision, and a proverb of reproach:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐροῦσιν ἐν ἑαυτοῖς μετανοοῦντες, καὶ διὰ στενοχωρίαν πνεύματος στενάξονται Οὗτος ἦν ὃν ἔσχομέν ποτε εἰς γέλωτα καὶ εἰς παραβολὴν ὀνειδισμοῦ,

Douay-Rheims

Saying within themselves, repenting, and groaning for anguish of spirit: These are they, whom we had some time in derision, and for a parable of reproach.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

dicentes intra se, pœnitentiam agentes, et præ angustia spiritus gementes: Hi sunt quos habuimus aliquando in derisum, et in similitudinem improperii.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:4.

We fools accounted his life madness, and his end to be without honour:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

οἱ ἄφρονες· τὸν βίον αὐτοῦ ἐλογισάμεθα μανίαν καὶ τὴν τελευτὴν αὐτοῦ ἄτιμον·

Douay-Rheims

We fools esteemed their life madness, and their end without honour.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Nos insensati, vitam illorum æstimabamus insaniam, et finem illorum sine honore;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:5.

How is he numbered among the children of God, and his lot is among the saints!

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

πῶς κατελογίσθη ἐν υἱοῖς θεοῦ, καὶ ἐν ἁγίοις ὁ κλῆρος αὐτοῦ ἐστιν;

Douay-Rheims

Behold how they are numbered among the children of God, and their lot is among the saints.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

ecce quomodo computati sunt inter filios Dei, et inter sanctos sors illorum est.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:6.

Therefore have we erred from the way of truth, and the light of righteousness hath not shined unto us, and the sun of righteousness rose not upon us.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἄρα ἐπλανήθημεν ἀπὸ ὁδοῦ ἀληθείας, καὶ τὸ τῆς δικαιοσύνης φῶς οὐκ ἔλαμψεν ἡμῖν, καὶ ὁ ἥλιος οὐκ ἀνέτειλεν ἡμῖν·

Douay-Rheims

Therefore we have erred from the way of truth, and the light of justice hath not shined unto us, and the sun of understanding hath not risen upon us.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ergo erravimus a via veritatis, et justitiæ lumen non luxit nobis, et sol intelligentiæ non est ortus nobis.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:7.

We wearied ourselves in the way of wickedness and destruction: yea, we have gone through deserts, where there lay no way: but as for the way of the Lord, we have not known it.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἀνομίας ἐνεπλήσθημεν τρίβοις καὶ ἀπωλείας, καὶ διωδεύσαμεν ἐρήμους ἀβάτους, τὴν δὲ ὁδὸν Κυρίου οὐκ ἔγνωμεν.

Douay-Rheims

We wearied ourselves in the way of iniquity and destruction, and have walked through hard ways, but the way of the Lord we have not known.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Lassati sumus in via iniquitatis et perditionis, et ambulavimus vias difficiles: viam autem Domini ignoravimus.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:8.

What hath pride profited us? or what good hath riches with our vaunting brought us?

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

τί ὠφέλησεν ἡμᾶς ἡ ὑπερηφανία; καὶ τί πλοῦτος μετὰ ἀλαζονίας συμβέβληται ἡμῖν;

Douay-Rheims

What hath pride profited us? or what advantage hath the boasting of riches brought us?

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Quid nobis profuit superbia? aut divitiarum jactantia quid contulit nobis?

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:9.

All those things are passed away like a shadow, and as a post that hasted by;

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

παρῆλθεν ἐκεῖνα πάντα ὡς σκιὰ καὶ ὡς ἀγγελία παρατρέχουσα·

Douay-Rheims

All those things are passed away like a shadow, and like a post that runneth on,

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Transierunt omnia illa tamquam umbra, et tamquam nuntius percurrens,

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:10.

And as a ship that passeth over the waves of the water, which when it is gone by, the trace thereof cannot be found, neither the pathway of the keel in the waves;

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὡς ναῦς διερχομένη κυμαινόμενον ὕδωρ, ἧς διαβάσης οὐκ ἔστιν ἴχνος εὑρεῖν, οὐδὲ ἀτραπὸν τρόπιος αὐτῆς ἐν κύμασιν·

Douay-Rheims

And as a ship that passeth through the waves: whereof when it is gone by, the trace cannot be found, nor the path of its keel in the waters:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

et tamquam navis quæ pertransit fluctuantem aquam, cujus cum præterierit non est vestigium invenire, neque semitam carinæ illius in fluctibus;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:11.

Or as when a bird hath flown through the air, there is no token of her way to be found, but the light air being beaten with the stroke of her wings and parted with the violent noise and motion of them, is passed through, and therein afterwards no sign where she went is to be found;

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἢ ὡς ὀρνέου δυπτάντος ἀέρα οὐθὲν εὑρίσκεται τεκμήριον πορείας, πληγῇ δὲ μαστιζόμενον ταρσῶν πνεῦμα κοῦφον καὶ σχιζόμενον βίᾳ ῥοίζου, κινουμένων πτερύγων διωδεύθη, καὶ μετὰ τοῦτο οὐχ εὑρέθη σημεῖον ἐπιβάσεως ἐν αὐτῷ·

Douay-Rheims

Or as when a bird flieth through the air, of the passage of which no mark can be found, but only the sound of the wings beating the light air, and parting it by the force of her flight; she moved her wings, and hath flown through, and there is no mark found afterwards of her way:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

aut tamquam avis quæ transvolat in aëre, cujus nullum invenitur argumentum itineris, sed tantum sonitus alarum verberans levem ventum, et scindens per vim itineris aërem: commotis alis transvolavit, et post hoc nullum signum invenitur itineris illius;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:12.

Or like as when an arrow is shot at a mark, it parteth the air, which immediately cometh together again, so that a man cannot know where it went through:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἢ ὡς βέλους βληθέντος ἐπὶ σκοπὸν τμηθεὶς ὁ ἀὴρ εὐθέως εἰς ἑαυτὸν ἀνελύθη, ὡς ἀγνοῆσαι τὴν δίοδον αὐτοῦ·

Douay-Rheims

Or as when an arrow is shot at a mark, the divided air presently cometh together again, so that the passage thereof is not known:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

aut tamquam sagitta emissa in locum destinatum, divisus aër continuo in se reclusus est, ut ignoretur transitus illius:

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:13.

Even so we in like manner, as soon as we were born, began to draw to our end, and had no sign of virtue to shew; but were consumed in our own wickedness.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

οὕτως καὶ ἡμεῖς γενηθέντες ἐξελίπομεν, καὶ ἀρετῆς μὲν σημεῖον οὐδὲν ἔσχομεν δεῖξαι, ἐν δὲ τῇ κακίᾳ ἡμῶν κατεδαπανήθημεν.

Douay-Rheims

So we also being born, forthwith ceased to be: and have been able to shew no mark of virtue: but are consumed in our wickedness. Such things as these the sinners said in hell:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

sic et nos nati continuo desivimus esse; et virtutis quidem nullum signum valuimus ostendere, in malignitate autem nostra consumpti sumus. Talia dixerunt in inferno hi qui peccaverunt:

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:14.

For the hope of the ungodly is like dust that is blown away with the wind; like a thin froth that is driven away with the storm; like as the smoke which is dispersed here and there with a tempest, and passeth away as the remembrance of a guest that tarrieth but a day.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι ἐλπὶς ἀσεβοῦς ὡς φερόμενος χνοῦς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου, καὶ ὡς πάχνη ὑπὸ λαίλαπος διωχθεῖσα λεπτή, καὶ ὡς καπνὸς ὑπὸ ἀνέμου διεχύθη, καὶ ὡς μνεία καταλύτου μονοημέρου παρώδευσεν.

Douay-Rheims

For the hope of the wicked is as dust, which is blown away with the wind, and as a thin froth which is dispersed by the storm: and a smoke that is scattered abroad by the wind: and as the remembrance of a guest of one day that passeth by.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

quoniam spes impii tamquam lanugo est quæ a vento tollitur, et tamquam spuma gracilis quæ a procella dispergitur, et tamquam fumus qui a vento diffusus est, et tamquam memoria hospitis unius diei prætereuntis.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:15.

But the righteous live for evermore; their reward also is with the Lord, and the care of them is with the most High.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

δίκαιοι δὲ εἰς τὸν αἰῶνα ζῶσιν, καὶ ἐν Κυρίῳ ὁ μισθὸς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἡ φροντὶς αὐτῶν παρὰ Ὑψίστῳ.

Douay-Rheims

But the just shall live for evermore: and their reward is with the Lord, and the care of them with the most High.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Justi autem in perpetuum vivent, et apud Dominum est merces eorum, et cogitatio illorum apud Altissimum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:16.

Therefore shall they receive a glorious kingdom, and a beautiful crown from the Lord’s hand: for with his right hand shall he cover them, and with his arm shall he protect them.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διὰ τοῦτο λήμψονται τὸ βασίλειον τῆς εὐπρεπείας καὶ τὸ διάδημα τοῦ κάλλους ἐκ χειρὸς Κυρίου, ὅτι τῇ δεξιᾷ σκεπάσει αὐτούς, καὶ τῷ βραχίονι ὑπερασπιεῖ αὐτῶν·

Douay-Rheims

Therefore shall they receive a kingdom of glory, and a crown of beauty at the hand of the Lord: for with his right hand he will cover them, and with his holy arm he will defend them.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Ideo accipient regnum decoris, et diadema speciei de manu Domini: quoniam dextera sua teget eos, et brachio sancto suo defendet illos.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:17.

He shall take to him his jealousy for complete armour, and make the creature his weapon for the revenge of his enemies.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

λήμψεται πανοπλίαν τὸν ζῆλον αὐτοῦ, καὶ ὁπλοποιήσει τὴν κτίσιν εἰς ἄμυναν ἐχθρῶν·

Douay-Rheims

And his zeal will take armour, and he will arm the creature for the revenge of his enemies.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Accipiet armaturam zelus illius, et armabit creaturam ad ultionem inimicorum.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:18.

He shall put on righteousness as a breastplate, and true judgment instead of an helmet.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἐνδύσεται θώρακα δικαιοσύνην, καὶ περιθήσεται κόρυθα κρίσιν ἀνυπόκριτον·

Douay-Rheims

He will put on justice as a breastplate, and will take true judgment instead of a helmet.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Induet pro thorace justitiam, et accipiet pro galea judicium certum;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:19.

He shall take holiness for an invincible shield.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

λήμψεται ἀσπίδα ἀκαταμάχητον ὁσιότητα,

Douay-Rheims

He will take equity for an invincible shield:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

sumet scutum inexpugnabile æquitatem.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 5:20.

His severe wrath shall he sharpen for a sword, and the world shall fight with him against the unwise.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:16.

She entered into the soul of the servant of the Lord, and withstood dreadful kings in wonders and signs;

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

εἰσῆλθεν εἰς ψυχὴν θεράποντος Κυρίου, καὶ ἀντέστη βασιλεῦσιν φοβεροῖς ἐν τέρασι καὶ σημείοις.

Douay-Rheims

She entered into the soul of the servant of God, and stood against dreadful kings in wonders and signs.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Intravit in animam servi Dei, et stetit contra reges horrendos in portentis et signis.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:17.

Rendered to the righteous a reward of their labours, guided them in a marvellous way, and was unto them for a cover by day, and a light of stars in the night season;

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ἀπέδωκεν ὁσίοις μισθὸν κόπων αὐτῶν, ὡδήγησεν αὐτοὺς ἐν ὁδῷ θαυμαστῇ, καὶ ἐγένετο αὐτοῖς εἰς σκέπην ἡμέρας καὶ εἰς φλόγα ἄστρων τὴν νύκτα.

Douay-Rheims

And she rendered to the just the wages of their labours, and conducted them in a wonderful way: and she was to them for a covert by day, and for the light of stars by night:

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Et reddidit justis mercedem laborum suorum, et deduxit illos in via mirabili: et fuit illis in velamento diei, et in luce stellarum per noctem;

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:18.

Brought them through the Red sea, and led them through much water:

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διεβίβασεν αὐτοὺς θάλασσαν ἐρυθράν, καὶ διήγαγεν αὐτοὺς δι᾽ ὕδατος πολλοῦ·

Douay-Rheims

And she brought them through the Red Sea, and carried them over through a great water.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

transtulit illos per mare Rubrum, et transvexit illos per aquam nimiam.

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:19.

But she drowned their enemies, and cast them up out of the bottom of the deep.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

τοὺς δὲ ἐχθροὺς αὐτῶν κατέκλυσεν, καὶ ἐκ βάθους ἀβύσσου ἀνέβρασεν αὐτούς.

Douay-Rheims

But their enemies she drowned in the sea, and from the depth of hell she brought them out. Therefore the just took the spoils of the wicked.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

Inimicos autem illorum demersit in mare, et ab altitudine inferorum eduxit illos. Ideo justi tulerunt spolia impiorum,

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:20.

Therefore the righteous spoiled the ungodly, and praised thy holy name, O Lord, and magnified with one accord thine hand, that fought for them.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

διὰ τοῦτο δίκαιοι ἐσκύλευσαν ἀσεβεῖς, καὶ ὕμνησαν, Κύριε, τὸ ὄνομα τὸ ἅγιόν σου, τήν τε ὑπέρμαχόν σου χεῖρα ᾔνεσαν ὁμοθυμαδόν·

Douay-Rheims

And they sung to thy holy name, O Lord, and they praised with one accord thy victorious hand.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

et decantaverunt, Domine, nomen sanctum tuum, et victricem manum tuam laudaverunt pariter:

↩

The Wisdom of Solomon 10:21.

For wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of them that cannot speak eloquent.

Greek (Septuagint / Swete)

ὅτι ἡ σοφία ἤνοιξεν στόμα κωφῶν, καὶ γλώσσας νηπίων ἔθηκεν τρανάς.

Douay-Rheims

For wisdom opened the mouth of the dumb, and made the tongues of infants eloquent.

Latin (Clementine Vulgate)

quoniam sapientia aperuit os mutorum, et linguas infantium fecit disertas.]
